raw.content:
A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were elevated, but nasopharyngeal Mycoplasma PCR was negative. Toxocara serology was sent and was pending at discharge.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 34-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman with a spontaneous dichorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy was transferred at 31 weeks 5 days’ gestation. Dichorionicity had been confirmed on first-trimester ultrasound. Pregnancy complications included early-onset growth restriction in twin 2 and new-onset preeclampsia at 30 weeks. At 16 weeks, ultrasound showed twin 1 with normal growth and normal amniotic fluid; twin 2 had estimated fetal weight <5th percentile, anhydramnios, and an absent bladder. Confirmatory ultrasound at 19 weeks revealed Tetralogy of Fallot in twin 2. By 21 weeks, twin 2’s amniotic fluid improved from anhydramnios to oligohydramnios (maximum vertical pocket 1.9 cm), and later normalized in both twins. Invasive testing was declined initially; at 31 weeks, chorionic villus sampling of twin 2 showed a normal chromosomal microarray.  
At 32 weeks, ultrasound at the tertiary center demonstrated:  
• Twin 1: estimated fetal weight 1904 g (62nd centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity (MCA-PSV) 26 cm/s (0.56 multiples of the mean).  
• Twin 2: estimated fetal weight 1128 g (<5th centile), normal amniotic fluid, normal umbilical-artery Dopplers, and MCA-PSV 50.9 cm/s (1.3 MoM).  
Placental imaging showed a normal-appearing placenta for twin 1 and a thickened, echogenic placenta for twin 2. These findings prompted suspicion for twin anemia-polycythemia sequence and an emergency cesarean section at 32 + 2 weeks.

A 41-year-old woman with a 3-month history of sacroiliac pain, arthralgias, and lower-limb myalgias partially responsive to NSAIDs was diagnosed with seronegative spondyloarthropathy (negative HLA-B27) after MRI confirmed bilateral active sacroiliitis. Two months later, she began weekly subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg with significant improvement in her joint symptoms. After the third dose, she developed a dry cough and dyspnea on moderate exertion without fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or other systemic symptoms. She denied tobacco use, recent travel, or exposures to animals, dusts, or sick contacts. 

On examination in the emergency department, she was afebrile, blood pressure 118/84 mmHg, pulse 96 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygenation normal on room air. Pulmonary auscultation revealed scant basal “Velcro”-like crackles. Other exams were unremarkable apart from positive sacroiliac provocation tests. 

Laboratory studies: Hb 13 g/dL, WBC 4,100/mm³ (neutrophils 2,000, lymphocytes 1,400), eosinophils 50/mm³, platelets 325,000/mm³; AST, ALT, bilirubin, creatinine, and BUN were within normal limits. 

High-resolution chest CT showed ground-glass interstitial infiltrates with a centrifugal distribution, predominantly in the upper lobes, and a mosaic pattern of disseminated attenuation without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. An echocardiogram was normal, and ECG showed sinus rhythm. 

Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage revealed no endobronchial lesions; GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis and methenamine silver stain were negative.

A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

raw.content:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

The owner reported that an esophageal obstruction had been suspected by the referring veterinarian, but spasmolytics and passage of a gastric tube did not improve the signs. On presentation, the llama was bright, alert, in good condition (body‐condition score 3.5/5) with normal vital signs. raw.content:
A 70‐year‐old woman with an undifferentiated connective tissue disorder and rheumatoid arthritis was treated with hydroxychloroquine in 2010, after which she developed a severe generalized bullous and pustular rash that resolved over three months following drug discontinuation and corticosteroid therapy. In 2022, hydroxychloroquine was restarted for her rheumatoid arthritis. Three days after restarting the drug, she was admitted with widespread erythema, desquamation, and pustulation. She denied any history of psoriasis. Laboratory studies revealed marked leukocytosis, hyperglycemia, hypoproteinemia, transaminitis, and an elevated C‐reactive protein level. Skin biopsies from the back demonstrated separation of the stratum corneum with multifocal subcorneal collections of neutrophils, underlying spongiotic epidermis with neutrophilic exocytosis, papillary dermal edema, and a superficial perivascular and interstitial infiltrate composed of lymphocytes, histiocytes, neutrophils, and rare eosinophils.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 24-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of progressive left hip pain radiating to the anterior thigh. The pain began as a dull aching groin discomfort, worsened over weeks, was severe at night, and was associated with weight loss and anorexia. There was no history of trauma. 

On examination, he had an antalgic gait, reduced range of motion of the left hip in all planes with spasms, and tenderness deep in the left groin. Straight-leg raising was negative, and neurologic examination was normal.

Laboratory studies, including complete blood count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein, were within normal limits. A pelvic radiograph was unremarkable. Initial MRI of the left hip showed synovitis and marrow edema without fracture. He received 6 months of empirical anti-tubercular therapy without clinical improvement.

An open synovial biopsy was performed; all cultures were negative, and histology showed mild to moderate chronic synovitis with lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates. Rheumatologic evaluation, including serologic studies, was unremarkable. A repeat MRI of the hips demonstrated a well-defined T1-hypointense, STIR-hyperintense lesion with a thick sclerotic rim in the anterolateral cortex of the left femoral head, associated marrow edema, moderate joint effusion, and synovitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 21-year-old man with no past medical or surgical history presented with a tender, palpable mass in his left buttock that he had noticed for several years but which had rapidly enlarged over the previous six months. He also reported recent onset of constipation and numbness of the left lower extremity, worsened by sitting. He denied any drainage, redness, fever, or systemic symptoms. He took no medications and had no family history of cancer.

On examination, a 4 × 4 cm tender mass was palpated in the left perineum without overlying skin changes. Neurologic examination showed hypoesthesia in the L5–S4 distribution on the left with intact motor function; the right lower extremity was normal. Abdominal and digital rectal examinations were unremarkable.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis revealed a well-defined, nonenhancing, unilocular hypodense cystic lesion anterior to the rectum measuring 7.0 × 9.0 cm, as well as a separate 4.4 × 4.7 cm cyst in the left perineum. On contrast-enhanced MRI, both lesions appeared homogeneous, T1 hypointense, T2 hyperintense, and showed no wall enhancement. The cysts were distinct from the bladder, urethra, prostate, and rectum, and were suggested to have a narrow neck traversing the pelvic floor near the pudendal canal.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Laboratory studies, including an infectious work-up, were negative.  
Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 39-year-old Ukrainian immigrant woman presented with approximately 1 year of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. She had no prior evaluations and was referred for upper endoscopy, which revealed a large antral mass; a mucosal biopsy was obtained, but she declined endoscopic ultrasound and was lost to follow-up during pregnancy. She later returned with ongoing anemia and new epigastric pain. Repeat esophagogastroduodenoscopy with endoscopic ultrasound identified a 6 cm mass arising from the muscularis propria of the gastric antrum. Preoperative computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 9.7 × 7.8 × 4.8 cm heterogeneous mass adherent to the posterior wall of the gastric antrum, with predominantly fat attenuation, internal septations, and no pathologic lymphadenopathy. She then presented with melena; a repeat endoscopy showed mucosal ulceration overlying the mass, and biopsy results were consistent with adipose tissue.

A 63-year-old woman presented with a one-year history of vague, colicky epigastric pain radiating to the interscapular region, associated with anorexia and malaise. The pain was relieved by changes in sitting position and worsened by eating. There was no history of alcohol use, abdominal trauma, or pancreatitis. Routine laboratory studies showed thrombocytosis (platelet count >1 000 000/µL) and elevated blood urea. Aspirin (80 mg daily) was initiated for presumed essential thrombocytosis. 

An abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a cystic lesion in the head of the pancreas. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen confirmed a well-circumscribed, 11.8 cm cystic mass in the pancreatic head, without invasion of adjacent organs or lymphadenopathy. The serum CA 19-9 level was within the normal range. 

On physical examination, vital signs were normal. The abdomen was soft and non-distended, with mild epigastric tenderness on deep palpation but no rebound or rigidity. There were no signs of portal hypertension or history of prior abdominal surgery.

raw.content:
A 75-year-old woman, previously well, transferred her care to a new general practitioner in June 2022. She reported a presumed stroke in April 2020 with slurred speech, imbalance, and confusion lasting 48 hours; at that time, brain MRI showed chronic periventricular white matter changes without acute ischemic lesions, and CT angiography demonstrated carotid tortuosity with stenosis from myointimal plaques. Her medications included barnidipine 20 mg daily, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, and atorvastatin 20 mg daily.

Since 2020, she experienced recurrent dizzying attacks characterized by sudden subjective vertigo, absence of nausea or vomiting, and unsteadiness with a wide-based gait requiring support; episodes lasted days to weeks and gradually resolved. Symptomatic treatments for dizziness were ineffective. Over months, attacks increased in frequency and duration until dizziness became constant, leading to loss of autonomy.

At the first visit, general and neurologic examinations were normal, and she reported a low mood. Days later, a severe attack prevented her from getting out of bed, prompting a home visit. Vital signs were normal; she was alert, oriented, and cooperative with normal speech. She described severe dizziness worsened by any movement or position change, without nausea or vomiting. With assistance, she sat on the bed with difficulty maintaining trunk control. When upright, she adopted a wide-based stance, was unsteady, and required external supports to walk. Romberg’s test was positive, with marked unsteadiness on eye closure. Strength and sensation were intact, reflexes were normal, and cranial nerves were intact. The finger–nose test was weakly positive on the right. The HINTS examination was negative.

A diagnostic algorithm for dizziness suggested a low probability of central or peripheral vestibular origin. Review of the CTA suggested that carotid stenosis had been overestimated due to marked vessel tortuosity. Transcranial Doppler confirmed tortuosity and plaques but demonstrated normal hemodynamics of the cerebro-afferent vessels. Repeat brain MRI showed no signs of recent vascular lesions.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 45-year-old man presented with a 5-day history of an abrupt onset of an asymptomatic cutaneous eruption on the neck and both forearms. The lesions began small and progressively enlarged over 5 days. He denied fever, malaise, or other constitutional symptoms, and reported no contact with cattle or sheep. He took no medications and had no significant medical history.

On examination, there were multiple papules and plaques of varying sizes on the dorsal forearms and nape of the neck, each showing a striking central depression that mimicked vesiculation; some neck lesions had an overlying crust. All lesions were firm and nontender. 

A Gram stain of fluid from one lesion was inconclusive. A punch biopsy showed no epidermal changes and revealed a dense inflammatory neutrophilic infiltrate within the dermis, marked dermal edema, and no evidence of vasculitis. 

Laboratory studies showed a hemoglobin level of 14 g/dL, a white-cell count of 13,000/mm3 with 89% neutrophils, and a normal peripheral smear. Renal and liver function tests were within normal limits. Imaging of the abdomen and pelvis was unremarkable. Urine testing for Bence–Jones protein was negative. A throat swab grew only normal flora.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 35-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder and chronic joint pain presented with a 15-month history of swelling and redness of her hands. She reported no precipitating factors, including temperature changes. She had occupational exposure to pool chemicals but noted no improvement with glove use. She described chronic joint pain in her hands and back. Prior treatments with topical mupirocin and emollients were unsuccessful. She denied coagulopathy but endorsed a 4-year history of injecting heroin, buprenorphine, suboxone, and morphine without tourniquet use into multiple sites, including the dorsal hands, wrists, and forearms. Three years after cessation of intravenous drug use, she experienced intermittent, painless, symmetric swelling of both hands. Two years later, during the second trimester of pregnancy, she developed persistent hand and foot edema with new erythema and was hospitalized for cardiac and thrombosis evaluation. An echocardiogram showed a normal ejection fraction; no diagnosis was made. Eleven months postpartum, examination revealed bilateral dorsal hand erythema and edema sharply demarcated at the wrists. Punch biopsy showed small‐vessel ectasia and minimal perivascular lymphocytes. Laboratory studies demonstrated negative antinuclear antibody, extractable nuclear antigen panel, and rheumatoid factor. Creatine kinase and aldolase were mildly elevated. Six-month–old creatinine levels, hepatic function tests, and hepatitis panels were normal.

raw.content:
A 19-month-old boy was brought to the emergency department after an episode of reduced consciousness while bathing. His parents reported that when lukewarm water was poured over his chest, he turned blue around the lips and began gasping for air. During this time, his eyes “rolled back,” and he did not interact with his parents. There were no clonic movements, and he did not respond to physical stimulation. He subsequently fell asleep for approximately 1 hour and was brought to the ED.

On arrival, he was alert and appeared well. There were no focal findings on examination, his development was appropriate, and laboratory studies—including a blood glucose level of 5.5 mmol/L—were normal. His parents reported similar, less profound episodes during bathing over the previous 2 weeks, in which his head would go back, his eyes would roll upward, and he would become floppy and limp for 2–3 minutes, followed by sleepiness. These episodes occurred only during bathing; contact with water in other settings did not provoke symptoms. He had normal developmental milestones and no significant past medical or family history.

An electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm with a normal QT interval. Bathing in lukewarm water while his vital signs were monitored provoked hypotonia, tachycardia, and brief apnea with associated desaturation. He stared straight ahead and made mouthing movements; he was removed from the bath, given high-flow oxygen, and again slept for about 1 hour. A further similar episode occurred later while he was sleeping, without any provocation. The first interictal EEG was normal using the standard 10–20 system. Because he was clinically well between episodes and there was an avoidable trigger, he was discharged with plans for follow-up investigations, including a brain MRI, a bathing EEG, and outpatient review.

A 64-year-old woman with a 20-year history of hypertension presented with dizziness and head discomfort of 3 days’ duration. Her blood pressure at presentation was 190/100 mmHg. She had no gastrointestinal symptoms (no abdominal pain, melena, hematemesis, or dysphagia).

An abdominal ultrasound was performed to evaluate her hypertension and incidentally revealed a 4.7 cm × 4.4 cm hypoechoic lesion with a clear, regular boundary located between the upper pole of the spleen and the abdominal aorta, without detectable blood flow. The radiologist noted that the lesion appeared to originate from the stomach and suggested a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST).

After blood-pressure control, she was admitted for further evaluation. Vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examination was unremarkable, and routine blood tests, blood biochemistry, fecal occult blood, and tumor markers were all normal.

Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT showed a 5.5 cm × 4.3 cm smoothly marginated soft-tissue mass in the gastric wall protruding beyond the serosal contour, with marked enhancement and surrounding lymph-node enlargement (nodes up to 1.0 cm). Malignancy, including GIST with nodal metastases, could not be excluded.

Upper endoscopy revealed a smooth, hemispherical submucosal elevation on the gastric fundus. Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a 3.7 cm × 4.4 cm hypoechoic, heterogeneous mass arising from the muscularis propria, with no internal vascularity.

EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration obtained scant gastric mucosal tissue and few spindle cells with areas of calcification, raising the possibility of a spindle cell tumor but without definitive typing. A second EUS-FNA was performed, yielding similar findings.

raw.content:
A 44-year-old woman from Veracruz, Mexico, of low socioeconomic status, with systemic lupus erythematosus since 2003 (cutaneous, joint, and renal involvement), presented with a one-week history of progressive headache, phonophobia, high-grade fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. One month earlier, she had been treated for SLE-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone at 1 mg/kg per day.

On admission she had systemic inflammatory response syndrome and nuchal rigidity but no focal neurologic deficits or clinical signs of lupus activity. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, eosinophils 150 cells/mm3, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, haptoglobin 77 mg/dL, ALT 59 IU/L, AST 78 IU/L, LDH 310 mg/dL, C3 96.5 mg/dL, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and proteinuria 310 mg/day. Chest radiograph and head CT were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed a pH of 7.35, glucose 45 mg/dL (serum glucose 130 mg/dL), protein 329 mg/dL, 42 white cells/mm3 (95% neutrophils), and 2 red cells/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Enterococcus gallinarum, and she was treated with intravenous ampicillin, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms.

On hospital day 3, she developed hemoptysis, bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, a drop in hemoglobin concentration, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. Cultures were obtained, and she was started on methylprednisolone boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

On hospital day 4, she developed a purpuric skin rash, and a skin biopsy was performed.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 38-year-old Indian man with a history of recurrent low-grade fevers and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus treated with metformin presented with 10 days of right-sided chest and right upper abdominal pain and dyspnea. He described sharp, tearing, localized pain (7/10), worsened by movement and deep inspiration, without cough or hemoptysis. He denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, sick contacts, recent travel, or asbestos exposure. He reported past extramarital sexual relationships. On admission: temperature 37.2°C; heart rate 110 bpm; blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Examination revealed a patchy, macular hyperpigmented rash on both shins and dorsum of the feet, and decreased breath sounds and vocal fremitus at the right lower chest. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 12.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelets 219 × 10^3/µL; blood urea nitrogen 4.3 mmol/L; creatinine 69 µmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy infiltrates in the right lower zone and obliteration of the right costophrenic angle. Thoracentesis yielded pale yellow fluid with 1260 WBCs/µL (87% neutrophils), 1590 RBCs/µL, pH 7.237; a rare giant cell was seen; cultures were negative. Pleural biopsy showed empyema without granulomas; Quantiferon and acid-fast bacilli studies were negative. CT chest revealed multiple encysted pleural effusions in the right lung. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no thrombi or intracardiac masses. A comprehensive respiratory viral and atypical pathogen panel was negative. The patient was treated sequentially with piperacillin/tazobactam and then meropenem, with gradual resolution of fever and clinical improvement; a chest tube and thoracotomy were performed to drain the effusion.

A 43-year-old man presented with fever, chills, and headache. One month earlier, he had noted a painless ulcer on the prepuce that was healing when he developed fever and fatigue. Ten days before admission, he developed a disseminated maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He reported multiple unprotected sexual contacts over the past three months. He is a man who has sex with men and was diagnosed with HIV infection 10 years ago; he takes abacavir, lamivudine, darunavir, ritonavir, and dolutegravir with an undetectable viral load and a CD4 count of 1144 cells/μL. One year ago, he was treated with intravenous penicillin G for suspected otosyphilis and had a full clinical and serologic response. 

On examination, he was ill-appearing but not dehydrated. He had painless enlargement of inguinal, axillary, and cervical lymph nodes (up to 3 cm) and a maculopapular rash on the trunk and extremities. He had a headache but no nuchal rigidity or Kernig or Brudzinsky signs.

Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 63,300/mL with a lymphomonocytic predominance. Blood urea nitrogen, creatinine, and urine specific gravity were within normal limits. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed 19 white cells (95% lymphocytes) with normal glucose and protein concentrations. Blood cultures were repetitively negative.

A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of gradually progressive swelling, pain, and stiffness in her left lower leg. She reported pain at rest and denied fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, or syncope. Her medical history was notable for three prior abortions, recurrent microcytic anemia treated with iron supplementation, and two prior dilation and curettage procedures. She had no personal history of DVT and no family history of thromboembolic disease.

On examination, her temperature was afebrile, heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The left lower leg was tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses were palpable, and sensation was intact without ischemic changes.

Laboratory studies showed normal renal function, electrolytes, C3, C4, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time; hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL with an MCV of 63 fL; C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (normal); and ESR 40 mm/hr (elevated). ECG and chest radiograph were normal. Doppler ultrasonography of the left lower extremity demonstrated extensive deep vein thrombosis. A porto-venous phase CT scan revealed compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery with a filling defect in the dilated, nonenhancing left common iliac vein. Given her obstetric history, tests for anti-beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, and antiphospholipid antibodies were sent, all of which returned negative.

A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 14-year-old Caucasian girl was transferred from a community emergency department after treatment for presumed anaphylaxis following ingestion of a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. Immediately after ingestion she reported wheezing, cough, and swelling of the lips, face, and tongue and self-administered epinephrine (0.3 mg) at home. Her history included suspected food allergies (wheat, oats, tree nuts, chocolate, eggs, cow’s milk, and rice) without documented reactions; intermittent asthma; complex regional pain syndrome; delayed gastric emptying; and major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine, increased to 60 mg daily 5 months earlier. Skin prick tests and serum-specific IgE to foods of concern were negative except for sensitization to several tree nuts without a supportive history of reaction with ingestion. Testing for hereditary angioedema and baseline serum tryptase were normal. She had lost 40 lb over the past year through dietary restriction and exercise and was homeschooled due to fears of allergic reactions.

In the ED she had stridor, biphasic wheezing, and poor air movement without visible oropharyngeal swelling. She was afebrile, blood pressure 94/48 mmHg, heart rate 100 bpm, respiratory rate 30/min, and SpO₂ 100% on room air. She received IV fluids, two doses of subcutaneous epinephrine, inhaled bronchodilators, racemic epinephrine, and antihistamines, and was admitted to the PICU. Her presumed angioedema resolved with treatment.

Over the next several weeks in an eating-disorder program, she had seven similar episodes requiring ED evaluation and PICU admission. Each episode featured subjective perioral swelling, hypotension within her baseline range, and stridor that resolved without objective edema. Direct laryngoscopy during one episode showed no airway edema or paradoxical vocal cord motion. Serial serum tryptase levels during acute events remained normal, a bone marrow biopsy was equivocal, and further workup—including complement levels, mast cell mediators, urine prostaglandins, complete blood count, and metabolic panel—was unremarkable. She was managed with daily antihistamines, ranitidine, cromolyn, and a tapering course of prednisone; rescue therapy included cetirizine and lorazepam. She continued to experience suicidal ideation and auditory hallucinations and was started on aripiprazole.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 35-year-old West African man with no prior psychiatric or medical history presented to clinic with a 1-week history of escalating behavioral changes. His family reported episodes of talkativeness, incoherent speech, visual and auditory hallucinations, insomnia, and grandiose and persecutory delusions. He denied head injury, substance use, or stressors and had no family history of psychiatric illness. He worked as a mechanical engineer in a mining community with potential mercury exposure and had no systemic or respiratory symptoms despite known community spread of COVID-19.

On examination he was afebrile, BP 135/80 mmHg, pulse 88 bpm, and with normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation. General and neurologic exams were unremarkable. He appeared disheveled, restless, and agitated but was oriented to time, place, and person. Speech was loud and clear without latency. He exhibited circumstantial thought, grandiose delusions (“I am a prophet of God”), persecutory delusions, and both auditory (“gunshots”) and visual (a mob) hallucinations. Memory was intact and he had no insight.

Laboratory studies showed a normal CBC, renal function, and albumin; γ‐glutamyl transferase was elevated at 81 IU/L (normal < 55) and total bilirubin 26 μmol/L (normal 3.4–20.5). Malaria and typhoid screens were negative. Urinalysis revealed transient proteinuria and glycosuria that normalized on repeat. Head CT scan was normal. A lateral flow COVID-19 antigen test and confirmatory RT-PCR were both positive.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

raw.content:
A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A copper intrauterine device had been removed 2 months before her last menstrual period. She had used one cycle of clomiphene. She had no chronic illnesses, did not smoke or drink, and was not on medications.

On examination, blood pressure was 113/70 mmHg, pulse 98 beats/min, and temperature 37.5 °C. Abdominal, cardiorespiratory, neurological, and pelvic examinations were unremarkable. Transvaginal ultrasound showed a 13 mm gestational sac with irregular margins and a yolk sac in the anterior isthmic portion of the uterus, raising suspicion for a cesarean-section scar ectopic pregnancy. Doppler was declined. Serial β-hCG measurements rose by 33% over 48 hours (21,521 mIU/mL). The patient missed follow-up and returned 1 week later with 5 days of worsening pelvic pain.

Repeat transvaginal scan revealed a fetal pole with cardiac activity (crown–rump length 0.9 cm) in a sac traversing the full width of the anterior myometrium, extending exophytically toward the serosa, with trophoblastic flow on Doppler; there was no endometrial fluid or free pelvic fluid. She was taken to laparoscopy and hysteroscopy: the bladder was densely adherent to the anterior uterine wall, the ectopic was not visualized, and extensive intrauterine adhesions obscured the view; there was no intracavitary bleeding. Postoperatively, she became hypotensive (systolic 82–95 mmHg) without vaginal bleeding. This prompted an urgent MRI to map the location of the pregnancy.

raw.content:
An 84-year-old Asian man was admitted with dyspnea and found to have a large recurrent right-sided pleural effusion—his third since starting empiric RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) nine months earlier for presumed extrapulmonary tuberculosis despite negative cultures and imaging. The initial colonoscopic biopsy showed granulomas with an acid-fast stain–positive organism, but cultures were negative; subsequent biopsies and sputum cultures have remained negative and QuantiFERON-TB Gold testing was negative. 

Four weeks after starting RIPE, he developed dyspnea, cough, and weakness and was hospitalized for a large right effusion. Thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocyte-predominant fluid with red color; stains and cultures were negative. He was diagnosed with a paradoxical tuberculous effusion and given systemic corticosteroids while continuing RIPE. 

Two months later, he represented with a similar effusion; repeat thoracentesis again yielded an exudative lymphocyte-predominant fluid, culture-negative. 

Two weeks later, a third re-accumulation prompted video-assisted thoracoscopic pleural biopsy. Pleural fluid showed lymphocytosis (96%), exudative protein and LDH, an adenosine deaminase of 23.8 U/L, and a low complement activity (CH50 10). Cytology was benign. Multiple pleural biopsies showed inflammation without granulomata; all cultures were negative. The pleural fluid ANA was negative. Serum testing revealed an ANA titer of 1:160 with a speckled pattern and a negative antihistone antibody assay.

raw.content:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 36 weeks 3 days of gestation presented with acute left lower abdominal pain and vomiting. She denied vaginal bleeding, urinary symptoms, constipation, or changes in bowel habits. Her observations were stable, and she appeared clinically well. On examination, there was slight tenderness in the left abdomen without guarding; the uterus was soft and relaxed. Foetal movements and monitoring were normal.

Her antenatal course had been uneventful except for a 70 × 60 × 60 mm left ovarian cyst first noted at 5 weeks and thought to be endometriotic. Follow-up scans at 32 weeks showed the cyst measured 63 × 33 × 69 mm with internal echoes and an avascular solid component. Tumour markers (CEA, CA-19-9, CA-125) were within normal limits, and an MDT review deemed the cyst benign and recommended surveillance.

On admission, Hb was 121 g/L, WCC 10.0 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 9.1 × 10^9/L, platelets 270 × 10^9/L, and CRP 30 mg/L. Over three days, CRP rose to 209 mg/L while WCC remained stable. Repeated transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasounds by an experienced sonographer showed the left adnexal cyst unchanged in size and appearance with no whirlpool sign, stromal oedema, absent Doppler flow, or free pelvic fluid. MRI was considered but not performed due to the rapid clinical change.

At 37 weeks 1 day, her pain worsened with vomiting, and abdominal exam revealed generalized tenderness with guarding in the left iliac fossa. Given the acute abdomen, rising inflammatory markers, and concern for ovarian torsion, the decision was made to proceed with a caesarean section followed by surgical management of the adnexa.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 35-year-old man from rural north India presented with a one-month history of a progressively enlarging, central abdominal lump. Three weeks after the lump appeared, he developed intermittent high-grade fever and dull, aching abdominal pain. He had no significant past medical history. On examination, there was a moderately tender mass in the umbilical region. There was non-tender thickening of the right spermatic cord without scrotal or testicular abnormalities; inguinal nodes were barely palpable, and there was no lower-extremity edema. Complete blood counts and blood chemistry were within normal limits, and blood cultures were sterile. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed a large, well-defined, unilocular cyst measuring 20 × 14 × 23 cm located behind the right colon and terminal ileum, without features suggestive of an abscess; the remainder of the abdominal organs appeared normal. Contrast-enhanced CT scan confirmed these findings but did not clarify the origin or etiology of the cyst. Because of diagnostic uncertainty and ongoing symptoms, the abdomen was explored surgically, revealing a large retroperitoneal cyst posterior to the right colon, mesocolon, and terminal ileum that stretched adjacent structures; a well-defined avascular plane allowed complete excision of the cyst, and a conglomeration of grossly dilated lymphatics near its upper pole was also removed.

raw.content:
A 66-year-old white man presented to the Emergency Department with abrupt onset of dyspnea, palpitations, and lightheadedness. In the ED, he was found to be in monomorphic ventricular tachycardia and was electrically cardioverted into normal sinus rhythm. His medical history included a cerebrovascular accident, Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene mutations, hypertension, incidentally noted pulmonary nodules, and chronic kidney disease (baseline GFR 40–45 mL/min/1.73 m2). He was taking losartan and warfarin and had no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Initial laboratory studies were within normal limits, and coronary angiography ruled out ischemia. His electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemic changes, but an epsilon wave in V1, a QRS duration of 140 ms, and T-wave inversions in leads V1–V5. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed preserved left ventricular function and no valvular disease, but a markedly dilated right ventricle with severely reduced systolic function. Based on an epsilon wave in V1–V3, T-wave inversions in V1–V3 with QRS >110 ms, an RV outflow tract dimension >32 mm, and severe RV dilation and hypokinesia, arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia was highly suspected. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging was indicated but not performed because of chronic kidney disease and patient preference. A septal endomyocardial biopsy was considered but deferred due to its low yield. Given the patient’s pulmonary nodules, cardiac sarcoidosis remained in the differential diagnosis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. At 22, she had trochanteric bursitis and an X-ray showed a Q-angle of 17°; no metabolic evaluation was done. She takes OTC vitamin D3 without calcium. She is 155 cm tall, weighs 58.5 kg (BMI 23.8), with no personal or family history of fractures or metabolic bone disease.

On exam, there is marked bilateral valgus alignment (left > right) with a knocking gait. Repeat X-ray shows a Q-angle of 23°. Bone density scanning reveals osteopenia of the left femoral head and normal lumbar spine density. Laboratory studies show:
• Serum phosphate: low  
• Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable  

A 24-hour urine collection demonstrates inappropriately normal phosphate excretion for the degree of hypophosphatemia and normal urine calcium. Renal ultrasound reveals bilateral medullary nephrocalcinosis without stones.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 49-year-old woman of African origin presented with a 10-year history of a right‐sided scalp mass that had been stable and nontender until it was excised at a peripheral clinic 5 months ago (no histopathology was done). Over the next 5 months, the lesion recurred, gradually enlarged, ulcerated, and bled easily. She denied headaches, convulsions, or neurologic deficits. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no pallor, jaundice, or palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Local scalp examination revealed two lesions on the right side: a fungating, tender, 9 × 7 cm mass prone to bleeding and mild mobility, and a second non‐fungating, 3 × 3 cm lesion. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel. Chest radiography and abdominal/pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. A head and neck CT scan demonstrated a multilobulated, hyperdense, ulcerative right frontal scalp lesion measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, along with enlarged cervical lymph nodes at levels I and II. MRI of the spine revealed a pathological compression fracture of T10 and a hyperintense lesion in T8, raising suspicion for vertebral metastases. Clinical staging was considered stage IVc.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 78-year-old man presented with a 4-week history of productive cough, occasional hemoptysis, and epistaxis. His medical history included hypertension and treated tuberculosis; he was an ex–cigarette smoker. Physical examination was unremarkable. A chest radiograph showed a spiculated 3.5 cm mass in the right lower zone. CT of the thorax demonstrated a 5 cm cavitating mass in the right lower lobe with bilateral small cavitating nodules. Laboratory tests revealed a cytoplasmic ANCA titre of 1 / 20 and a PR3 level of 14.6 IU ml−1. CT-guided biopsy of the right lower lobe mass showed necrotizing granulomatous inflammation without evidence of malignancy. The patient was started on subcutaneous methotrexate, and after 3 months a chest radiograph showed reduction of the nodule to 2 cm. He then developed renal impairment attributed to disease progression and/or methotrexate toxicity, and treatment was switched to high-dose intravenous cyclophosphamide with a tapering dose of oral prednisolone. After 3 months of cyclophosphamide, he developed a new cough and chest radiography showed enlargement of the right lower lobe nodule to 4 cm; CT confirmed an increase to a 5 cm cavitating mass at the same location.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 51-year-old man presented with a 1-year history of gradually progressive pain and swelling below his left knee, accompanied by intermittent fevers. Three months before presentation, the swelling ulcerated. He remained ambulatory without assistance.  
On examination, there was a firm mass measuring 30 × 18 × 12 cm over the distal tibia extending into the calf, with an anterior discharging ulcer 12 cm in diameter and areas of necrosis. The discharge was yellow and thick. Knee range of motion was reduced, and there was tenderness over the left knee and proximal tibia. Distal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial, popliteal) were intact and lower-limb neurologic examination was normal. Other systemic examination findings were unremarkable.  
Laboratory studies, including complete blood count and metabolic panel, were within normal limits. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Plain radiographs of the left leg demonstrated a large metadiaphyseal lesion of the tibia with soft-tissue opacity, bone erosion and destruction of the tibia and adjacent fibula, and linear and ring-like calcifications, with extension into the proximal leg soft tissues. A Tc-99m bone scan revealed increased tracer uptake in the shaft of the left tibia and proximal soft tissue, without evidence of distant skeletal metastases. MRI was not obtained due to financial constraints.  
Based on the clinical presentation and radiographic appearance, the leading considerations were osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma of the tibia. On admission, the patient received intravenous antibiotics and analgesics and was counseled regarding treatment options. Taking into account lesion size, secondary infection, prosthesis cost, and prognosis, the patient elected transfemoral amputation with plans for postoperative chemotherapy.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 14-year-old boy was referred from a mission hospital for postoperative wound sepsis after right scrotal exploration and orchidectomy for testicular torsion. He had 24 h of scrotal pain and swelling before surgery. On arrival he was tachypneic, tachycardic (124 bpm), febrile (38.7 °C), and diaphoretic, with pallor of mucous membranes. Blood pressure was 109/68 mmHg, neck veins were flat, and heart sounds were normal. The tips of his fingers and toes appeared cyanosed bilaterally with peripheral oxygen saturations fluctuating between 20% and 30% on room air, despite no severe dyspnea. Ecchymoses were present over the extremities, and he bled easily from puncture sites. The right groin wound appeared necrotic and septic. He had no chronic illnesses or medications and denied smoking.  

Initial laboratory studies showed white blood cells 16 × 10^3/µL with neutrophils 10.8 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 4.8 g/dL, and platelets 26 × 10^3/µL; liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, malaria smear, and hemoglobin electrophoresis were normal. A diagnosis of severe sepsis complicated by DIC and anemia was made, and he received broad-spectrum antibiotics, blood and platelet transfusions, and surgical debridement.  

Despite improvement in systemic parameters and extubation on day 6, cyanosis of fingers and toes progressed to well-demarcated gangrene below the elbows and knees. A contrast angiogram of the aorta and its branches showed patent thoracic and abdominal aorta and no filling defects in major limb arteries.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 81-year-old Asian man with erectile dysfunction, CKD stage 3a (baseline creatinine 1.4 mg/dL, eGFR 47 mL/min/1.73 m2), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, coronary artery disease, gout on long-term allopurinol, and osteoarthritis presented with one month of generalized edema and a 9.1 kg weight gain. On admission: BP 144/70 mmHg, exam notable for diffuse bilateral lower extremity edema; cardiac and lung exams unremarkable. Chest radiograph showed small bilateral pleural effusions. Renal ultrasound was normal without hydronephrosis. Echocardiogram: EF 68% with normal structure.  

Laboratory studies: WBC 5.4 × 10^9/L with 5.6% eosinophils; serum BUN 48 mg/dL; creatinine 3.7 mg/dL; albumin 2.6 g/dL. Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.020, 4+ blood, 4+ protein. Sediment: 0–2 granular casts/high-power field, 0–5 RBCs/hpf, 0–1 WBC/hpf.

A 60-year-old man with a 14-year history of polycythemia vera and hypertension was admitted with acute severe abdominal pain, nausea, and transient loss of consciousness. He reported vague abdominal discomfort intermittently over the past decade. His medications included aspirin, hydroxyurea, and intermittent losartan; he had poor adherence to phlebotomies and other therapy. On arrival, blood pressure was 110/75 mmHg; he was lethargic and confused. Physical examination showed epigastric and periumbilical tenderness, splenomegaly, and left costovertebral-angle tenderness. Laboratory studies were notable only for chronic leukocytosis consistent with his underlying disease; other values were within normal limits. 

An abdominopelvic CT scan with contrast demonstrated splenomegaly and a 40 × 23 mm hypodense lesion in the right adrenal gland (55 HU) and a 60 × 35 mm ill-defined lesion in the left adrenal gland, without evidence of vascular thrombosis. Two days later, after supportive care, an adrenal-protocol CT showed persistent massive splenomegaly (25 cm) and bilateral adrenal masses (right 40 × 29 mm, left 48 × 26 mm) that were nonenhancing with an attenuation of 50 HU.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 56-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-week history of dry cough and mild weight loss. She denied fever, haemoptysis, night sweats, and had no known contacts with tuberculosis. Two courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, coarse crepitations were heard over the right upper and lower lung zones. A chest radiograph showed an air-space opacity in the right upper lobe. CT of the thorax demonstrated multifocal consolidations in the right upper lobe extending to the right lower lobe. Given the clinical and radiographic suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis, she was started empirically on anti-tuberculosis therapy. After 2 weeks, her symptoms persisted. A Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed 10 mm of induration. Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli was negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Xpert® Mycobacterium tuberculosis/rifampicin assay as well as bacterial and fungal cultures. Hence, a CT-guided lung biopsy was planned.

raw.content:
A female infant was delivered at 26 weeks and 6 days of gestation to a healthy 26-year-old primigravida mother after an uneventful pregnancy until 19 weeks, when routine ultrasound identified a 34×28 mm sacrococcygeal mass with internal and external components. Amniocentesis showed a normal array comparative genomic hybridization, and a fetal echocardiogram was normal. At 22 weeks, MRI demonstrated a 60×70×57 mm sacrococcygeal mass with mixed features—predominantly solid with a 40 mm cyst—and no invasion or compression of pelvic structures or the coccyx (Altman type II). Subsequent ultrasounds showed rapid growth to 80×60 mm with profuse vascularization.

Spontaneous vaginal delivery occurred after antenatal steroids. The infant’s birth weight was 1300 g, and Apgar scores were 0, 0, and 5 at 1, 5, and 10 minutes. She required positive-pressure ventilation with FiO₂ up to 1.0 and intravenous adrenaline, with return of heart rate after 6 minutes. A single dose of surfactant was administered.

On admission to the NICU, vital signs were: heart rate 103/min, respiratory rate 70/min, blood pressure 19/15 mm Hg (mean 17), and axillary temperature 34.1 °C. She was ventilated on SIMV with volume guarantee (PIP 25 cm H₂O, PEEP 5 cm H₂O, rate 70/min, FiO₂ 1.0, VG 6 mL/kg). Physical examination revealed pallor, prolonged capillary refill, and a 14×7×4 cm, approximately 750 g, reddish sacrococcygeal mass with visible active bleeding. Initial management included repeated saline and glucose boluses, transfusion of red blood cells (30 mL/kg), fresh-frozen plasma (10 mL/kg), and platelets (10 mL/kg). Post-transfusion hemoglobin remained 5.8 g/dL. Severe metabolic acidosis was noted (pH 6.80, HCO₃⁻ 8.6 mmol/L, base excess −25).

A 30-year-old man with no prior medical or psychiatric history presented with sudden onset of painless bilateral loss of vision immediately after falling approximately 3 meters from a pickup truck, resulting in a concussion and a superficial scalp laceration. One hour after injury, he was alert and oriented (Glasgow Coma Scale score 15) and had visual acuity of counting fingers bilaterally. Systemic and neurologic examinations were otherwise unremarkable. The following day, visual acuity was no light perception in both eyes. Anterior and posterior segment examinations, relative afferent pupillary defect testing, fogging test, and menace reflex were all normal. Noncontrast computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no abnormalities. Visual evoked potentials were normal, and electroretinography indicated no pathologic process. In view of these inconclusive findings, the patient was referred for psychiatric evaluation to rule out conversion disorder.

raw.content:
A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

A 70-year-old man with castration-resistant prostate cancer and a 4-year history of diabetes mellitus presented with painless purpura on his fingertips. His prostate cancer, which had recurred with bone metastases after multiple radiotherapy and chemotherapy regimens, was found to harbor a BRCA1 mutation. Two months before presentation, he began olaparib at 600 mg/day. One month after starting olaparib, he developed nonpalpable, faint purpura on the fingertips that gradually spread to other fingers. 

On examination, there were disseminated, faint, nonpalpable purpura confined to the fingertips, with no other skin findings. He denied pain or other systemic symptoms. Laboratory studies showed a white-cell count of 2,900/mL, hemoglobin 11.1 g/dL, and platelet count 123,000/mL; a similar low platelet count had been noted 5 years earlier.

raw.content:
A 68-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis and a 1-month history of mild cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Mild wheezing was auscultated bilaterally; neurologic and skin findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 72-year-old man with a history of stage IIIA gastric cancer treated by distal gastrectomy and adjuvant S-1 six months previously developed peritoneal and para-aortic lymph-node recurrence treated with weekly paclitaxel. After seven courses of chemotherapy, he experienced progressive anorexia and general fatigue and was referred for further evaluation.

On admission, he was alert. Temperature was 38.5 °C, blood pressure 110/53 mmHg, heart rate 64 beats/min, weight 60.2 kg (BMI 22.3 kg/m2). He had no skin or mucosal hyperpigmentation and normal pubic and axillary hair. Chest and abdominal examinations were unremarkable.

Laboratory tests showed: WBC 1.97×103/µL with neutrophils 350/µL, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, platelets 199×103/µL; CRP 3.1 mg/dL; blood glucose 101 mg/dL; electrolytes on admission normal (Na 141 mEq/L, K 4.1 mEq/L, Cl 101 mEq/L). CT scans showed no progression of lymph-node metastases or ascites, and no focus of infection.

He was treated for febrile neutropenia with G-CSF: his neutrophil count and fever improved within three days, but his anorexia and fatigue worsened, rendering him bedridden. One week after admission, his ECOG performance status declined from 2 to 4. On hospital day 5, laboratory tests revealed Na 122 mEq/L, serum osmolality 239 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 482 mOsm/kg. Fluid intake was restricted to 1 L/day for presumed SIADH, but the hyponatremia persisted.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 59‐year‐old Japanese woman was referred for 6 weeks of bilateral posterior ankle pain and anterior knee pain, and 4 weeks of pain in the metacarpophalangeal joint of the left third finger. She had been diagnosed with hypertension and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) at age 57, with an initial LDL‐C of 359 mg/dL, reduced to ~170 mg/dL on pitavastatin and ezetimibe for the past 6 months. She had no personal or family history of rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she had bilateral arcus corneae; swelling and thickening of the midportion of both Achilles tendons with tenderness to palpation extending to the calcaneal insertion; tenderness over both tibial tuberosities and the right medial humeral epicondyle; and tenderness of the first and fifth right MTP joints and the second left MTP joint. The right third and right second MCP joints were swollen dorsally, and a nodule was noted on the extensor tendon of the right third digit. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 118 mm/h, CRP 2.06 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor 49.3 U/mL (normal <15), anti‐CCP2 >300 U/mL (normal <4.5), and MMP‐3 62.3 ng/mL (normal <59.7). Radiographs of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees showed no erosions or enthesophytes, although the ankle films demonstrated soft‐tissue widening suggestive of Achilles tendon thickening. Musculoskeletal ultrasound revealed the following:
- Achilles tendons: markedly swollen, rounded cross‐section; inhomogeneous, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed markedly increased vascularity inside and around the tendon, with vessels entering from the ventral aspect via Kager’s fat; no paratenon thickening, bursitis, or bony irregularity.  
- Patellar tendons: focal thickening of the distal tendon, inhomogeneous hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow in hypoechoic areas; no bursitis or bony changes; mild suprapatellar synovitis.  
- Finger extensor tendons at the right third and left second and fourth MCP joints: focal thickening, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow; mild synovitis in the right second MCP joint.  
- Feet: synovial thickening with hyperemia in the first, second, third, and fifth MTP joints of the right foot and the first and second MTP joints of the left foot.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

raw.content:
A 40-year-old man presented with 5 days of progressive dyspnea. On day 1 he was short of breath only with uphill walking (MMRC grade 1), by day 2 he was breathless on level ground (grade 2), and by day 4 he was dyspneic at rest (grade 4). He also noted central, nonradiating chest pain with coughing, without positional change. He denied fever, night sweats, cyanosis, grunting, palpitations, or hemoptysis. He had three previous hospital admissions, most recently 4 months earlier for acute severe pancreatitis. He had a 5-year history of local alcohol consumption but had abstained for 6 months. 

On examination, pulse was 116/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 98 °F, and SpO2 95% on 4 L O2 by nasal prong. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees. Chest inspection showed decreased movement on the left; trachea deviated rightward; decreased fremitus and stony dullness over the entire left hemithorax; and absent breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, WBC 5530/mm3, CRP 73.9 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L, serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, serum amylase 486 U/L, and lipase 416 U/L. 

Chest radiograph revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal shift to the right, consistent with massive left pleural effusion. 

Ultrasonography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large left pleural effusion with passive basal lung collapse, and showed a normal-sized pancreas with heterogeneous echotexture and a small intrapancreatic collection at the tail. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple non-enhancing cystic areas in the pancreas (largest 23×16 mm in the tail), minimal peripancreatic fat stranding, and no main pancreatic duct dilation or parenchymal calcifications. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded 900 mL of dark brown, turbid fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 3.5 g/dL; LDH 1413 U/L; glucose 98 mg/dL; ADA 31.4 U/L; total cell count 100/mm3 (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes); amylase 11,871 U/L; PCV 0.8%; no malignant cells; culture negative; MTB/RIF PCR negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
